title: The Distant Interior
premise: Petra Whitlock, a translator who has spent three years avoiding the language of her childhood—Kavreni, spoken by a community her father's mining company helped displace—is summoned by Mirela, its last fluent speaker, to become her final student. Returning to the valley where the story went wrong, Petra discovers that Mirela's request is not nostalgia but testimony: she wants the language carried out of the valley so that what was buried there, including the truth about a death Petra's family caused, can finally be spoken aloud. As Mirela's health fails and local interests move to silence the last witness, Petra must choose between the invisibility that has protected her and the justice that lives only in words. The novel ends with Mirela's death and Petra, now the sole speaker, delivering the language—and the confession it carries—to a courtroom of no jurisdiction but a full room: the displaced community itself.
about_author: Astrid Almeida is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages and one silence. She writes about translation as an act of witness and lives near a river whose original name she is still learning.

chapters.title: The Art of Almost
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. In Lisbon, Petra works translating corporate contracts, deliberately declining jobs involving Kavreni while privately hoarding borrowed words in a notebook she never rereads. A letter arrives from Mirela Duarte, the last speaker, asking for one final student before winter. Emotional beat: the comfort of avoidance cracking into dread and longing.

chapters.title: What the Valley Keeps
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra travels back to the northern valley, finding the resettlement town built over the old village and the mine her father's company opened. Mirela receives her coolly, testing her with phrases Petra half-remembers. Emotional beat: shame surfacing as homecoming; the past made physical in landscape.

chapters.title: First Lessons
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, interleaved with Mirela's teaching voice. Lessons begin: not vocabulary but ways of seeing—Kavreni has no word for 'own,' only for 'keep for a while.' Petra learns the language encodes a different relationship to property and power. Emotional beat: wonder shadowed by guilt, as each lesson implicates her further.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. In the town archive, Petra finds the displacement documents bearing her father's signature—and a reference to a protest, a fire, and a death ruled accidental: Tomás Reis, a Kavreni elder. She realizes Mirela knew him intimately. Emotional beat: the discovery that her family name sits at the center of the wound.

chapters.title: Mirela's Terms
chapters.summary: Mirela's POV. Mirela reveals why she summoned Petra specifically: not forgiveness, but strategy. A development consortium is moving to pave the old village site, which would erase the last physical evidence. She needs a speaker who can carry testimony out before both she and the ground are gone. Emotional beat: cold clarity hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra's brother Daniel arrives, representing the consortium, offering Mirela money and Petra a partnership—both designed to buy silence. Petra refuses him publicly in imperfect Kavreni, her first spontaneous speech in the language. Emotional beat: the exhilaration and terror of choosing a side out loud.

chapters.title: The Fire, Retold
chapters.summary: Mirela's POV. Mirela tells the true story of the night Tomás died—not an accident but a deliberate clearing operation—and reveals she recorded testimony for decades on tapes hidden beneath the chapel floor. Petra realizes the language itself is the evidence: idioms that preserve names, dates, accusations. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Winter Comes Early
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Mirela suffers a stroke; lessons become bedside vigils. Consortium lawyers file to declare the site historically insignificant, and someone breaks into Mirela's house searching for the tapes. Petra moves them, learning faster now because there is no time left. Emotional beat: desperation sharpening into fluency; love arriving too late to say easily.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker Speaks
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. At a public hearing meant to rubber-stamp the paving, Petra rises and gives Mirela's testimony in Kavreni, translating aloud sentence by sentence—the death, the signatures, her father among them. Daniel cannot stop her without confirming everything. Emotional beat: climax; the private art of almost saying becomes public saying.

chapters.title: Keep for a While
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Mirela dies at first snow, Petra holding her hand and speaking to her only in Kavreni. The hearing stalls the development; the tapes reach journalists and the displaced families. Petra stays, teaching a small class of grandchildren from a notebook she finally rereads. Emotional beat: quiet resolution—justice incomplete but begun, identity chosen rather than inherited.
